title: Burst mitigation sequencer field notes
content:
Summary:

This is a working notebook capturing the design, experiments and quick observations for the "sequencer" approach to handle short bursts that currently produce tail spikes in continuous-batching workloads. The goal: reduce transient p99/p999 latency regressions during traffic bursts while retaining high throughput and minimal average latency penalty.

Background / problem statement:
- We observe reproducible tail spikes (p99.9) on some tenant workloads when sudden request bursts arrive (10-100x baseline QPS for 100-500ms). Spikes manifest as batch formation stalls and kernel hot-spot contention producing long stalls on the GPU side.
- Existing heuristics (timeouts + max-batch-size) are brittle: either they flush too early (smaller batches -> cost/throughput regression) or they hold and create starvation + long tails.
- Hypothesis: a lightweight sequencer layer in front of the batcher that actively shapes admission during burst windows can smooth arrivals and avoid pathological flush/evict oscillations.

Sequencer concept (high-level):
- Inline, per-worker state machine that:
  1) Detects a burst window by short-term qps derivative and queue-occupancy gradient.
  2) Switches from normal passive coalescing to an active sequencing policy for a short epoch (e.g., 50-200ms).
  3) Emits small sub-batches at deterministic cadence (e.g., 4ms ticks) but allows priority reordering for urgent requests.
  4) Applies a token-smoothing budget so high-token requests don't monopolize a sequencer epoch.
- Key properties we want: graceful degradation, no global lock handoffs, per-worker bounded memory usage, compatibility with KV-cache prefix reuse.

Experiment matrix (what we ran):
- Workloads: two synthetic mixes derived from production traces: 
  A) Chatty-short: 8-20 token requests, high arrival burst (peak 80x baseline), low prefill usage.
  B) Long-prefill: 400-1200 token requests with long prefix reuse and bursty intermittent traffic.
- Baselines:
  - current-default (timeout=6ms, max_batch=128)
  - priority-preserve (same timeout but tenant priority preemption enabled)
- Sequencer variants (parameter sweep):
  S1: cadence 4ms, epoch 60ms, token_budget_per_epoch = 1024, allow_priorities=true
  S2: cadence 6ms, epoch 100ms, token_budget_per_epoch = 4096, allow_priorities=false
  S3: cadence 3ms, adaptive-cadence (based on instantaneous queue size), epoch 50ms
  S4: same as S3 but with prefill-awareness (prefer reusing KV-cache-prefilled requests at sequence start)
- Metrics captured: p50/p90/p95/p99/p99.9/p99.99, mean batch size, batch size histogram, kernel queue length, GPU SM utilization, CPU scheduler cycles, request queuing time, number of flushes per epoch, token throughput (tokens/sec), and cost proxy (tokens/GPU-second).

Profiling approach and tools:
- Flamegraphs for worker threads (user-space batcher + runtime goroutines).
- GPU traces from perf and CUPTI to map long kernel stalls to batch time windows.
- Microtrace correlation: tag requests with sequencer-epoch-id and propagate to microtrace to correlate per-request wait times with sequencer events.
- Synthetic injection harness to replay production bursts with controlled start/stop and configurable inter-arrival jitter.

Key observations (raw):
- On Chatty-short workload, baseline suffers p99.9 spikes of 220-350ms during the first 150ms of a burst. These correlated with a large flush that tried to include many requests but encountered a kernel warm- up stall and then queueing backpressure.
- Sequencer S1 reduced p99.9 to 42-70ms with only a 5% throughput drop. Mean batch size dropped 18% but variance dropped >60% (fewer giant batches).
- S2 (no priorities) performed worse on Long-prefill: we lost most KV-cache benefit and saw p95 regressions. Prefill-aware S4 recovered the p95 and reduced p99 by ~30% compared to baseline.
- Adaptive cadence (S3) shows promise: it keeps average batch size closer to baseline while keeping tails low, but it introduces complexity: cadence oscillation and a new source of scheduling jitter if not damped.

Root causes surfaced during profiling:
- Kernel eviction stalls: when a very large batch enters the GPU concurrently with kernel selection logic that triggers a specialized attention kernel, the runtime blocks subsequent smaller batches while memory barriers complete (observed as 30-80ms stalls). Sequencer reduces probability of this alignment.
- CPU-side queue lock contention in the flush path: many threads attempting to mark a batch as ready during a burst cause short but stacked mutex waits. Sequencer reduced the number of concurrent flushes, lowering contention.
- KV-cache churn: naive sequencing that emits fresh requests without considering prefills loses cache hits and increases per-token GPU work. 

Representative microtrace snippet (formatted):
- t=0ms burst start
- t=12ms sequencer epoch 1 emits sub-batch (size 12)
- t=13-18ms worker 2 flush -> kernel A chosen
- t=16ms sequencer epoch 2 emits sub-batch (size 9)
- t=18ms worker 5 flush -> short wait at kernel selection (locks) -> kernel B delayed 42ms
- result: request X p99 path took +58ms waiting for kernel B

Quantitative summary (selected):
- Chatty-short workload: baseline p99.9 = 320ms, S1 p99.9 = 48ms, throughput change = -5.2%
- Long-prefill workload: baseline p99 = 145ms, S4 p99 = 98ms, throughput change = -1.3% (within noise)
- Cost proxy: tokens/GPU-sec increased by 2.8% for S1 but decreased 0.6% for S4 (prefill-aware).

Operational considerations / risks:
- Sequencer adds state (epoch ids) and new per-worker timers; failure modes must be bounded: watchdog to force-evict if sequencer stalls.
- Interaction with autoscaling: sequencer reduces instantaneous queue depth, so downscalers might undershoot if they observe lower bursty metrics. Need to feed autoscaler with peak-aware signals or delay downscale window.
- Observability: we need to export sequencer metrics (epochs/sec, average cadence, evictions, priority defers) and attach epoch-ids to traces to make debugging workable in production.

Next steps / action items:
- Short term (2 weeks): harden S1 with watchdog and extended tracing; add epoch-id propagation to logs and open GH PR with sequencer toggle behind config flag.
  Owner: Alex Rivera
- Mid term (4-6 weeks): implement prefill-aware variant (S4) as default in the dedicated cluster for a small canary subset of tenants; add autoscaler hook to avoid premature downscales.
  Owner: Priya Nair
- Long term: consider a hybrid where the sequencer is only enabled when the system detects a burst pattern and then disabled after an epoch; add ML-based burst predictor to reduce false positives.
  Owner: Maya Chen / ML infra collaboration

Notes to self / scratch ideas (unstructured):
- Might be worth building a cheap hardware-aware kernel guard: if a queued batch will trigger a heavy kernel, delay it by a few ms and let lightweight ones pass. Need more kernel-level classification signal.
- Explore a permissive mode where the sequencer only tags but doesn't reorder for the first ramp to collect telemetry without risking regressed throughput.
- Check interaction with streaming responses (where early tokens are returned): ensure sequencing doesn't increase first-byte latency beyond SLOs.

Attached items / experiments referenced: 
- GH branch: sequencer/wip (link in linked_artifacts)
- Replay harness config ids: replay-2026-01-burstA, replay-2026-01-burstB
- Benchmark logs: /mnt/bench-archives/burst-seq-2026-01/ (internal only)

Questions unresolved:
- How to tune token_budget_per_epoch per tenant? static thresholds are brittle. Could we infer from recent token distribution windows?
- What's a safe default cadence for heterogeneous hardware fleets (A100 vs T4)? need per-hardware calibration.

If you want to run the short replay for S1 locally: 
1) checkout GH: redwood-inference/serving-runtime branch sequencer/wip
2) run: tools/replay --config replay-2026-01-burstA --sequencer-mode S1 --trace-tag "seq-test"
3) gather traces: tools/collect-traces --tag seq-test --out /tmp/seq-traces
4) look at aggregator: scripts/trace-aggregate --in /tmp/seq-traces --metrics p99,p999,mean-batch-size

End of notes.

(Leave as draft; will formalize into playbook once S4 validation completes.)
